title: Auricular Hematoma Drainage and Bolster
source_label: Pasha 6e (Otology and Head and Neck Trauma chapters)
indications: Any tense, fluctuant collection between perichondrium and auricular cartilage after blunt or shearing trauma (wrestling, boxing, rugby, falls), most often on the anterior surface where skin is tightly bound to perichondrium. Drain as soon as it is recognized, ideally within the first days, because the cartilage depends on the perichondrium for its blood supply; untreated or reaccumulated blood causes cartilage necrosis, perichondritis and fibrocartilaginous overgrowth (cauliflower ear). Very small, flat collections may be observed only if the patient can be rechecked closely. Needle aspiration may clear a small, fresh, liquid collection seen within the first day or two, but recurrence is higher, and once the blood clots and organizes (within days) incision and evacuation are needed.
setup: Usually a bedside or clinic procedure; patient supine or seated with the head turned and the ear well lit (headlight or loupes)
Ear ring block with local anesthetic (diamond pattern of about six injection points around the auricle) or targeted local infiltration
Prep the whole auricle and postauricular skin; keep the canal plugged with a cotton ball to keep prep and blood out

Tray: #15 blade, fine scissors, small curette or Freer, suction or syringe with saline, nylon or polypropylene through-and-through sutures, bolster material (dental rolls, petrolatum gauze, silicone sheets or thermoplastic splints)
Document hearing complaints and inspect the canal and tympanic membrane for associated injury before you start
Plan follow-up within 24 to 48 hours and again around day 7 before you begin
landmarks: Antihelix and its superior and inferior crura
Anterior perichondrium, tightly adherent to skin
danger: Cartilage necrosis from leaving blood or applying an overly tight bolster
Cutting through cartilage with a deep incision or curette
Incision across the helical rim, which leaves a visible notch
Dead space under the skin flap that allows reaccumulation
Missed perichondritis or abscess in a delayed presentation
Associated canal laceration, temporal bone fracture or ossicular injury
steps: Confirm the diagnosis

Distinguish a fluctuant, effaced auricle with loss of the normal folds from simple soft-tissue swelling or perichondritis. Note the size, location (scaphoid, triangular fossa, concha), and age of the collection, because blood older than about a week may be organized or loculated and harder to evacuate completely.
Anesthetize

Perform an ear ring block, injecting anterior, posterior, superior and inferior to the auricle so all sensory contributors are covered, then add local infiltration along the planned incision and in the concha, since the ring block may spare the conchal and canal territory of the auricular branch of the vagus (Arnold nerve). Avoid injecting directly into the collection, which distorts it and adds volume under the skin.
Plan the incision

Place the incision within a natural fold, usually parallel to and just inside the helical rim along the scaphoid fossa or in the antihelical fold, so the scar hides in shadow. Make it long enough to evacuate clot fully; a needle puncture alone rarely clears organized blood and recurrence is common.
Incise skin and perichondrium only

Cut through skin and the lifted perichondrium with a #15 blade, staying superficial to the cartilage. The perichondrium is the vascular lifeline for the cartilage, so it should be lifted with the skin as one layer, never stripped off separately.
Evacuate the clot

Express and gently curette the clot with a small curette or Freer, sweeping in all directions under the flap. Irrigate the pocket with saline until the return is clear and inspect for loculations. Remove any obviously organized or infected tissue, preserving viable cartilage.
Inspect the cartilage

Look at the exposed cartilage surface for fractures, devitalized fragments or neocartilage in a late presentation. Thickened, fibrotic tissue from a recurrent hematoma can be carefully shaved to restore contour, but avoid aggressive debridement of healthy cartilage.
Redrape the flap

Lay the skin-perichondrial flap back onto the cartilage and confirm that it conforms to every fold without a residual pocket. The incision can be left partly open or loosely approximated so any further ooze drains out rather than collecting beneath the flap.
Place the through-and-through bolster

Contour dental rolls or petrolatum gauze to the anterior concavity and to the posterior auricular surface, then pass several through-and-through mattress sutures of nylon or polypropylene through bolster, ear and bolster. This compresses the flap onto the cartilage and eliminates dead space; it is the key step against reaccumulation.
Check bolster tension

Tie the sutures snug enough to coapt the flap but not so tight that the skin blanches, because pressure necrosis of skin and cartilage is a real complication. Alternatives include silicone sheets or thermoplastic splints molded to both surfaces and secured with transcartilaginous sutures.
Apply an outer dressing
Fluff gauze behind the ear to support the auricle and wrap with a light mastoid dressing for the first day. Keep the ear protected from rubbing and from sleeping on the operated side.
Follow up and remove

Recheck within one to two days for pain, swelling or skin compromise, then remove the bolster at about 5 to 7 days. Examine for reaccumulation; a recurrent small collection can be re-drained and re-bolstered, and athletes should use protective headgear on return.
exit_check: Auricle contour restored with all folds visible and no residual fluctuance
Bolster sutures snug but skin perfused (pink, no blanching)
Canal checked and clear; follow-up for bolster check booked
postop: Keep the bolster dry and in place for about 5 to 7 days
Analgesia with acetaminophen or NSAIDs; avoid sleeping on the treated ear
Return immediately for increasing pain, redness, foul drainage or new swelling
No contact sport until the bolster is out and the ear is healed, then protective headgear
Counsel that recurrent untreated collections lead to permanent cauliflower deformity

early: Skin or cartilage pressure necrosis from a tight bolster
late: Visible scar or notch at the helical rim
Canal stenosis if the collection extended into the concha

attending_followup: Why is the anterior surface of the auricle the usual site of hematoma?
Anterior skin is tightly adherent to the perichondrium, so shearing forces separate perichondrium from cartilage there; posterior skin is loose and glides, so shear is absorbed.
What is the pathophysiology of cauliflower ear?

Blood separates the avascular cartilage from its perichondrial blood supply; cartilage necroses and the stimulated perichondrium lays down disorganized fibrous tissue and neocartilage, producing a thickened, deformed auricle.
Why is needle aspiration alone often inadequate?

Within days the blood clots and becomes gelatinous, so it does not aspirate fully, and without compression the dead space refills. Aspiration is reasonable only for a small, fresh, liquid collection, whereas incision with evacuation plus a bolster has lower recurrence.
Which pattern of injection anesthetizes the entire external ear?

An ear ring block, a diamond-shaped series of injections around the base of the auricle covering the auriculotemporal, great auricular and lesser occipital territories. The concha and canal, supplied partly by the auricular branch of the vagus (Arnold nerve), often need separate local infiltration.
What is the main risk of the bolster itself and how do you avoid it?
Pressure necrosis of skin and cartilage; tie the through-and-through sutures to coapt without blanching and recheck the ear within 24 to 48 hours.
